words.meaning: extreme tiredness caused by working too hard for too long
words.example: After six months of seventy-hour weeks, she hit total burnout and took a month off.

words.meaning: the quality of working hard and giving your time and energy because you care
words.example: His dedication to the project impressed the whole team.

words.meaning: to do two or more things at the same time
words.example: Most managers have to multitask between meetings, emails, and calls all day.

words.meaning: the amount of work a person has to do
words.example: The new system helped us share the workload more fairly.

words.meaning: an extra benefit you get from your job, besides your pay (informal)
words.example: One nice perk of the job is free lunch every Friday.

words.meaning: to meet and connect with people who can help you in your career
words.example: She networks at industry events to find new clients.

words.meaning: to make a big change in direction, especially in your career or business
words.example: After ten years in banking, he pivoted to teaching.

words.meaning: to grow, develop, and become very successful
words.example: She really thrives in a busy, creative office.

words.meaning: to give part of your work or responsibility to someone else
words.example: A good manager knows how to delegate tasks to the right people.

words.meaning: an important event or achievement in your work or life
words.example: Launching the app was a huge milestone for our small team.

grammar.title: 6B: Modals of deduction - might, can't, must
grammar.explanation:
Use **might**, **can't**, and **must** to guess about the present. You base your guess on what you see or know.

Use **might** when you think something is possibly true. Your new colleague **might** be tired; her workload looks very heavy.

Use **can't** when you are sure something is impossible. He **can't** be on holiday; his dedication keeps him at his desk every day.

Use **must** when you are sure something is true. They **must** be celebrating a milestone; everyone in the office is smiling.

The opposite of **must** is **can't**, NOT **mustn't**. Say 'She **can't** be the manager', not 'She **mustn't** be the manager'.

We often use **might**, **can't**, or **must** with be + -ing for actions happening now. 'They **must** be networking at the conference right now.'
examples: *She *might* be in a meeting.* (her calendar is full)
*He *can't* be the new intern.* (he looks too experienced)
*They *must* be working late.* (the office lights are still on)
*You *must* be tired after that workload.* (a kind guess)
*They *must* be having a party.* (the music is very loud)
*He *might* be looking for a better perk.* (he asked about benefits)
